title: CSS Selectors
summary: A selector tells CSS which HTML elements should receive a style.

subtopics.title: Element selector
subtopics.explanation: An element selector uses a tag name, such as `p`, to match paragraph elements. It is like addressing everyone with the same role. Use it for broad defaults, such as base text styles, and use component classes when different areas need distinct appearances.

subtopics.title: Class selector
subtopics.explanation: A class selector begins with a dot, such as `.card`, and matches elements with that class. One class can be reused on many cards. It is like a shared membership label. Classes are the usual choice for reusable component styles because they describe a role without requiring a unique element.

subtopics.title: ID selector
subtopics.explanation: An ID selector begins with `#`, such as `#main`, and matches an element with that ID. An ID should be unique on the page. It is like addressing one specific person. IDs are useful for anchors and scripting, while reusable visual styles usually belong in classes.

subtopics.title: Combine selectors
subtopics.explanation: A descendant selector uses a space to match an element inside another, such as `.menu a` for links inside a menu. It is like giving an instruction to items in one area. Keep selector chains short; a long chain can break when the markup structure changes.

subtopics.title: Rule priority
subtopics.explanation: Specificity helps determine which matching rule wins when rules set the same property. IDs generally outweigh classes, and classes generally outweigh element names; source order resolves some ties. It is like a priority system for competing instructions. Prefer simple selectors so overrides remain predictable.

foundations.overview: A CSS selector tells the browser which HTML elements should receive a style rule. It is like choosing which people receive a notice: everyone, a named group, or one specific person. Simple selectors are easier to maintain. Learn element, class, and ID selectors first, then combine them only when the relationship is meaningful. A matching selector does not guarantee its rule wins; the cascade also matters.
foundations.whyItMatters: Selectors define the reach of a style change. Predictable, low-specificity selectors reduce accidental effects across unrelated parts of a large interface.
foundations.browserPerspective: Browsers match selectors right-to-left for efficiency: for 'nav a', they first find all <a> elements (the key selector) and then check whether each has a nav ancestor. This is why overly deep selectors can be slower.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Component classes (.card, .btn), state styling (:hover, :focus), zebra-striped tables (:nth-child), styling form inputs by type ([type=...]), and scoping styles to a section (nav a) are all everyday selector use.
foundations.businessImpact: Maintainable selectors let teams ship UI changes quickly and confidently; brittle selectors cause regressions and slow development.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A clear selector strategy (class-first, shallow, intent-named) keeps specificity flat, making styles easy to reason about, override, and refactor at scale.
foundations.performanceImpact: Selector matching is usually cheap, but very deep or universal-heavy selectors across large DOMs add cost; key-selector-first matching means specific, shallow selectors perform best.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Browsers read selectors left-to-right like we do.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They match right-to-left, starting from the key (rightmost) selector, which is why deep descendant chains can be inefficient.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Ids are good for styling because they're specific.
commonMisconceptions.reality: High specificity makes ids hard to override; classes are preferred so specificity stays low and styles remain reusable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A more specific selector is always a better selector.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Specificity can make future overrides difficult; prefer the simplest selector that identifies the intended elements.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A class selector can match only one element.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The same class can be reused on many elements, which is why it suits component styles.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A longer selector is automatically more precise and maintainable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Long chains are fragile and can make overrides harder; choose the simplest clear selector.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An ID selector is ideal for every unique component style.
commonMisconceptions.reality: IDs are unique and often increase specificity; reusable classes are usually easier to maintain.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A descendant selector targets only direct children.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A space matches descendants at any depth; use `>` when only direct children should match.

interactiveExamples.title: Type, class, and id together
interactiveExamples.explanation: Three selectors target the same page: a type selector for all paragraphs, a class for the highlighted one, and an id for the unique title.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A blue title, a gray paragraph, and a highlighted (yellow) paragraph.

interactiveExamples.title: Combinators and pseudo-classes
interactiveExamples.explanation: A child combinator styles only top-level list items, and :nth-child stripes them, while :hover changes the color on mouseover.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A striped list whose items turn blue when hovered.

codeLab.title: Target elements precisely
codeLab.instructions: In styles.css, (1) make all links inside .nav blue, (2) make external links (href starting with https) bold, and (3) stripe the table rows using :nth-child. Edit only styles.css.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Blue nav links (the external one bold) and a table with striped odd rows.
hints: Use a descendant combinator (.nav a) for the first task.
Use an attribute selector with ^= for 'starts with', and :nth-child(odd) for striping.
